question:
Select the most appropriate option to substitute the underlined segment in the given sentence.
It is very hard for her to provide the necessities of her family.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 1 i.e. the necessities to her family.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The verb "provide" is correctly used in the structures "provide something to somebody" or "provide somebody with something". It is never followed by "of" before the person who receives the thing.

• Rule: Provide + object + to + person, OR Provide + person + with + object.

• Applying the rule, "the necessities of her family" must be corrected to "the necessities to her family", meaning she supplies the essential things needed by her family.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 1.

Additional Information

• Option 2: "the necessities by her family" is incorrect because "by" indicates the doer of an action, not the receiver of something that is provided.

• Option 3: "the necessity of her family" wrongly changes the plural noun "necessities" (the actual things needed) into the singular abstract noun "necessity" (the state of being necessary), which does not fit the sense of providing material things.

• Option 4: "the necessities from her families" is incorrect because "from" does not fit the "provide ... to" pattern, and "families" is wrongly pluralised when only one family is meant.

NOTE

• Similar verb-preposition pairs frequently tested by SSC: supply something to somebody, explain something to somebody, provide somebody with something, furnish somebody with something.

question:
The following sentence has been divided into four segments. Identify the segment in which the article has been used INCORRECTLY.
UNESCO works to / strengthen an intellectual / and moral solidarity / of humankind.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 1 i.e. strengthen an intellectual.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The adjectives "intellectual" and "moral" both describe the SAME single noun "solidarity" (one particular, specific kind of solidarity). When two adjectives jointly describe one single noun/idea, only ONE article is needed before the first adjective.

• Rule: When two or more adjectives qualify the same singular noun referring to one entity/idea, use only a single article before the first adjective; use the definite article "the" when a specific, particular instance is meant.

• Applying the rule: "an intellectual and moral solidarity" should correctly read "the intellectual and moral solidarity", since it refers to the one particular solidarity of humankind that UNESCO seeks to strengthen.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 1.

Additional Information

• Option 2: "of humankind." is correct as printed; "humankind" is an uncountable/collective noun and needs no article.

• Option 3: "UNESCO works to" is correct; "UNESCO" is a proper noun (name of an organisation) and takes no article.

• Option 4: "and moral solidarity" is not where the error lies; the faulty article "an" appears earlier, in segment 1, not in this segment.

NOTE

• When two adjectives describe two DIFFERENT nouns (e.g. "a black and a white dog" = two dogs), the article is usually repeated before each. When they describe the SAME noun/entity (e.g. "the Secretary and Treasurer of the club" = one person), only one article is used.

question:
Select the option that can be used as a one-word substitute for the given group of words.
The study of coins
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 1 i.e. Numismatics.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• "Numismatics" means the study or collection of coins, banknotes, medals and related objects. (सिक्कों के अध्ययन का विज्ञान)
◦ Example: He has been passionate about numismatics since childhood and owns coins from over forty countries.

• The word comes from the Latin "numisma", meaning "coin", combined with the suffix "-ics", denoting a field of study.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 1.

Additional Information

• Option 2: Choreography (नृत्य रचना कला): The art of designing and arranging sequences of steps and movements for a dance.

• Option 3: Informatics (सूचना विज्ञान): The science concerned with the processing, storage and retrieval of information/data.

• Option 4: Cartography (मानचित्र कला): The study and practice of drawing or making maps.

NOTE

• Other one-word substitutes frequently tested by SSC: Philately (study/collection of postage stamps), Numismatist (one who studies/collects coins), Epigraphy (study of inscriptions), Numerology (study of the mystical significance of numbers).

question: Select the INCORRECTLY spelt word.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 1 i.e. Eficient.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The correct spelling is "Efficient", with a double "f" — capable of achieving maximum productivity with minimum wasted effort or expense.
◦ Example: The new machine is far more efficient than the old one.

• Spelling key: EF + FI + CIENT. The word "Eficient" printed in the option is missing one of the two "f"s, which makes it incorrect.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 1.

Additional Information

• Option 2: "Contribution" is spelt correctly — the act of giving something to a common purpose.

• Option 3: "Miscalculation" is spelt correctly — an error made in calculating something.

• Option 4: "Mediation" is spelt correctly — intervention in a dispute to resolve it.

NOTE

• Words with doubled consonants are commonly tested for spelling errors by SSC: efficient, accommodation, occurrence, embarrassment, committee, necessary, possession. Always check whether a consonant is doubled or not.

question:
Select the option that can be used as a one-word substitute for the given group of words.
A person who is inclined to see the worst aspect of things
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 1 i.e. Pessimist.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• A "Pessimist" is a person who tends to see the worst aspect of things and expects the worst possible outcome. (निराशावादी व्यक्ति)
◦ Example: Being a pessimist, he always expects his plans to fail.

• The root "pessim-" comes from Latin "pessimus", meaning "worst", which directly matches the given definition.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 1.

Additional Information

• Option 2: Philanthropist (परोपकारी व्यक्ति): A person who seeks to promote the welfare of others, especially through the generous donation of money.

• Option 3: Optimist (आशावादी व्यक्ति): A person who is inclined to see the best aspect of things and expects the best possible outcome — the exact opposite of the given meaning.

• Option 4: Altruist (परहितकारी व्यक्ति): A person who is unselfishly concerned for the well-being of others.

NOTE

• Commonly confused opposite pair: Pessimist (worst-expecting) vs Optimist (best-expecting). Related words: Misanthrope (one who dislikes mankind), Cynic (one who believes people are motivated by self-interest).

question:
Select the option that expresses the given sentence in passive voice.
He will give a lecture on personality development.
option_1: A lecture on personality development can be given by him.
option_2: A lecture will be given on personality development.
option_3: A lecture on personality development will be given by him.
option_4: A lecture on personality development will be giving by him.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 3 i.e. A lecture on personality development will be given by him.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The sentence "He will give a lecture on personality development" is in the Simple Future Tense.

• Rule — Simple Future Tense:
◦ Active: Subject + will/shall + V1 + Object
◦ Passive: Object + will/shall + be + V3 + by + Subject

• Applying the rule: the object "a lecture on personality development" becomes the subject; the auxiliary "will be" is retained; the verb "give" becomes its past participle "given"; and "he" becomes the agent "by him".
◦ Passive: A lecture on personality development will be given by him.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 3.

Additional Information

• Option 1 is incorrect because "can be given" expresses ability/possibility (Modal "can"), not simple futurity as in the original sentence with "will".

• Option 2 is incorrect because it drops the agent "by him" entirely, changing the meaning of who will give the lecture.

• Option 4 is incorrect because "will be giving" is the wrong passive form (this looks like a faulty Future Continuous passive); the correct passive auxiliary structure is "will be + V3", i.e. "will be given", not "will be giving".

NOTE

• The passive of the Future Continuous Tense (Subject + will be + V-ing + Object) is not commonly formed in standard English and is rarely tested; always double check the auxiliary and the form of the main verb (V3, not V-ing) while converting a future-tense sentence to passive voice.

question:
Sentences of a paragraph are given below in jumbled order. Arrange the sentences in the correct order to form a meaningful and coherent paragraph. Note: This is an advertisement of an ice-cream brand.
(A) That's why Silky is deliciously different and exceptionally versatile, natural, thick and durable ice cream.
(B) Beautifully firm, nice, silky rather than thin and watery, it stays in shape and stands on top of fruits or pastries without soaking in.
(C) Silky thick double ice cream has a unique, fresh taste and texture.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 3 i.e. CBA.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• Sentence (C) is the best opening sentence — it introduces the product/topic ("Silky thick double ice cream") and states its unique taste and texture, which is what the whole paragraph then goes on to explain.

• Sentence (B) logically follows (C) — it elaborates on the texture just mentioned ("firm, nice, silky") using the pronoun "it", which refers back to the ice cream named in (C), and describes how it stays in shape.

• Sentence (A) is the concluding sentence — it begins with "That's why", a conclusive/summary connector that draws a conclusion from the qualities described in (C) and (B), and ends the advertisement with a punchy closing statement.

• Reading the sequence C-B-A together produces a coherent, logically flowing advertisement: product introduced, its texture explained, then a concluding claim.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 3 (CBA).

Additional Information

• Option 1 (ABC) is incorrect because it opens with the concluding connector "That's why" before the product or its qualities have even been introduced, which is illogical.

• Option 2 (BAC) is incorrect because it opens with the pronoun "it" in (B) before the noun it refers to ("Silky thick double ice cream" in C) has been introduced.

• Option 4 (BCA) is incorrect for the same reason as Option 2 — it begins with (B), whose pronoun "it" has no antecedent yet, since (C) has not appeared first.

NOTE

• In para-jumble questions, always look for: (i) the sentence that introduces the main subject/noun (usually the opening line), (ii) pronouns like "it", "they", "this" that must follow their antecedent noun, and (iii) connective/conclusive words like "therefore", "that's why", "thus", "hence" which almost always mark the concluding sentence.

question:
Select the most appropriate synonym of the given word.
Bully
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 4 i.e. Oppressor.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• "Bully" (as a noun) means a person who habitually seeks to harm, intimidate, or coerce those who are weaker. (दबंग/धौंसिया व्यक्ति)
◦ Example: The class bully used to snatch other students' lunch money.

• "Oppressor" means a person who treats others in a harsh, cruel and unjust manner, keeping them under subjugation (उत्पीड़क), which closely matches the sense of a "bully" — someone who dominates and mistreats others.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 4.

Additional Information

• Option 1: Plough (हल): A farming implement used for cutting furrows in soil — unrelated in meaning.

• Option 2: Oxen (बैल, plural of ox): A domesticated bovine animal used for farm labour — unrelated in meaning.

• Option 3: Coddle (लाड़-प्यार से पालना): To treat someone in an indulgent or overprotective way — this is nearly opposite to the harsh meaning of "bully".

NOTE

• Other synonyms of "bully": tyrant, intimidator, browbeater, persecutor. Do not confuse "bully" (verb: to intimidate) with "bull" or "bullion", which are unrelated words with similar spelling.

question:
Select the most appropriate synonym of the given word.
Thankful
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 3 i.e. Obliged.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• "Thankful" means feeling or expressing gratitude; pleased and relieved. (आभारी/कृतज्ञ)
◦ Example: She was thankful for the timely help she received from her neighbours.

• "Obliged" means feeling grateful for a favour or kindness received (आभारी/कृतज्ञ), which is the closest synonym of "thankful" among the given options.
◦ Example: I would be much obliged if you could help me with this work.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 3.

Additional Information

• Option 1: Ungrateful (कृतघ्न): Not feeling or showing gratitude — this is the direct antonym of "thankful", not a synonym.

• Option 2: Affirmation (पुष्टि): The act of confirming or asserting something is true — unrelated to gratitude.

• Option 4: Obscure (अस्पष्ट): Not clearly expressed or understood; unclear — unrelated in meaning.

NOTE

• Other synonyms of "thankful": grateful, appreciative, indebted. Its direct antonym is ungrateful/thankless.

question:
Select the most appropriate option to fill in the blank.
Ram went to _____ an ice cream.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 1 i.e. buy.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The blank requires a verb in its base form (infinitive without "to" already used) to complete the structure "went to + Verb", expressing the purpose of going. "Buy" (to purchase) is the only word among the options that is a verb and fits this sense.

• Rule: "went to" is followed by the base form of a verb (V1) to show purpose — went to buy, went to see, went to eat, etc.

• Applying the rule: "Ram went to buy an ice cream" correctly means Ram went with the purpose of purchasing an ice cream.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 1.

Additional Information

• Option 2: "by" is a preposition (meaning "next to" or indicating an agent/means) and cannot function as a verb here.

• Option 3: "byre" is a noun meaning a cowshed, and makes no sense in this context.

• Option 4: "bye" is an informal word of farewell (or a term in cricket/sport) and cannot be used as a verb after "went to".

NOTE

• "Buy", "by" and "bye" are commonly confused homophones (identical or near-identical in sound but different in meaning and spelling). Remember: buy = to purchase (verb), by = preposition, bye = farewell/a run in cricket not off the bat.

question:
The following sentence has been split into four segments. Identify the segment that contains an error.
Dr. Sinha has / brought about a new / book on social / impact of child labour.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 3 i.e. brought about a new.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The sentence is about the publication of a book, and the correct phrasal verb for publishing/releasing a book is "bring out", not "bring about".

• Rule (phrasal verbs): "Bring out" means to publish or release something (a book, a product); "bring about" means to cause something to happen (an event, a change).

• Since the sentence talks about Dr. Sinha publishing a book, the segment should read "brought out a new", not "brought about a new".

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 3.

Additional Information

• Option 1: "impact of child labour" is grammatically correct as printed and fits the sentence.

• Option 2: "book on social" is grammatically correct; "book on (a topic)" is a standard collocation.

• Option 4: "Dr. Sinha has" is grammatically correct; "has" correctly functions as the auxiliary for the Present Perfect Tense.

NOTE

• Commonly confused phrasal verbs with "bring": bring about (cause to happen), bring out (publish/reveal), bring up (raise a child/raise a topic), bring round (persuade someone; also, revive someone from unconsciousness), bring down (reduce; overthrow).

question:
Select the option that expresses the given sentence in passive voice.
His behaviour vexes me sometimes.
option_1: He is being vexing me with his behaviour
option_2: Sometimes he vexes me with his behaviour.
option_3: I am sometimes vexed by his behaviour.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 3 i.e. I am sometimes vexed by his behaviour.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The sentence "His behaviour vexes me sometimes" is in the Simple Present Tense, with "his behaviour" as subject and "me" as object.

• Rule — Simple Present Tense:
◦ Active: Subject + V1/V5 + Object
◦ Passive: Object + is/am/are + V3 + by + Subject

• Applying the rule: the object "me" becomes the subject "I", taking the auxiliary "am"; the verb "vexes" becomes the past participle "vexed"; and "his behaviour" becomes the agent introduced by "by"; the adverb "sometimes" is retained in its normal mid-sentence position.
◦ Passive: I am sometimes vexed by his behaviour.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 3.

Additional Information

• Option 1 is incorrect because it reverses subject and object (making "he" the subject) and also wrongly uses the continuous form "is being vexing", which is not valid passive voice and distorts the original meaning.

• Option 2 is incorrect because it is simply a reworded active-voice sentence with "he" as subject, not a passive-voice sentence at all.

• Option 4 is incorrect because it drops the object "me" entirely (no agent "by me"), so the sentence no longer conveys who is affected by the behaviour.

NOTE

• While converting active to passive, always check that (i) the tense is preserved, (ii) the original object becomes the new subject correctly, and (iii) the agent ("by + subject") is retained unless it is unimportant or obvious from context.

question: Select the sentence that contains a spelling error.
option_1: The host institution must provide the delegates with accomodation at a subsidised rate.
option_2: The occurrence of the lunar eclipse is often a mystery for children.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 1 i.e. The host institution must provide the delegates with accomodation at a subsidised rate.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The correct spelling is "accommodation", with a double "c" and a double "m" — a place to live, stay, or sleep; or arrangements/space provided for a purpose.

• Spelling key: AC + COMM + ODATION. The word "accomodation" printed in the sentence is missing one "m", which makes it incorrect.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 1.

Additional Information

• Option 2 is spelt correctly — "occurrence" (double "c", double "r") and "eclipse" are both correctly spelt.

• Option 3 is spelt correctly — "addressed" (double "d", double "s") is correctly spelt.

• Option 4 is spelt correctly — "parallel" (single "r", double "l") is correctly spelt.

NOTE

• Words with doubled consonants are a favourite SSC spelling trap: accommodation, occurrence, embarrassment, committee, recommend, necessary, parallel, address. Always check carefully which consonant is doubled and which is not.

question:
Select the most appropriate synonym of the given word.
Labour
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 2 i.e. Toil.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• "Labour" (as a noun/verb) means hard physical or mental work. (कड़ी मेहनत)
◦ Example: Years of hard labour went into building this house.

• "Toil" means exhausting physical or mental labour (कड़ा परिश्रम), and is the closest synonym of "labour" among the given options.
◦ Example: After years of toil, the farmer finally had a good harvest.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 2.

Additional Information

• Option 1: Mesh (जाल): A network of interlaced wire or thread, or to become entangled — unrelated in meaning.

• Option 3: Dalliance (चंचलता/खिलवाड़): A casual romantic or sexual relationship, or a brief flirtation with an idea — unrelated in meaning.

• Option 4: Relaxation (विश्राम): The state of being free from tension and anxiety; rest — this is nearly the opposite of "labour".

NOTE

• Other synonyms of "labour": exertion, drudgery, grind, industry. Its antonym is rest/relaxation/leisure.

question:
Select the most appropriate option that can substitute the underlined segment in the given sentence.
To the general public, William was best known as a crusader for peace and as an admired critic about social, political and ethical subjects.
option_1: for peace and as an admired critic by
option_2: for peace and as an admired critic on
option_3: about peace and as admired critic about
option_4: in peace and as an admired critic about
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 2 i.e. for peace and as an admired critic on.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The preposition "for" correctly follows "crusader" (a crusader FOR a cause, e.g. "a crusader for peace"), so this part of the underlined segment does not need to change.

• Rule (preposition after "critic"): When "critic" refers to someone who comments/writes on broad subjects or issues, the correct preposition is "on" (a critic on social/political subjects), not "about".

• Applying the rule: "an admired critic about social, political and ethical subjects" should correctly read "an admired critic on social, political and ethical subjects".

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 2.

Additional Information

• Option 1: "critic by" is incorrect; "by" does not fit after "critic" when referring to subjects commented upon.

• Option 3: "about peace... critic about" is incorrect on both counts — "crusader about peace" wrongly replaces the correct "crusader for peace", and "critic about" remains uncorrected.

• Option 4: "in peace... critic about" is incorrect — "crusader in peace" is not idiomatic (it should be "for peace"), and "critic about" remains uncorrected.

NOTE

• Commonly tested preposition collocations: crusader for (a cause), critic of/on (a subject or person's work), campaigner for, advocate of/for.

question:
Select the most appropriate meaning of the underlined idiom.
In those days, we did not expect luxuries; we were thankful if we could keep the wolf from the door.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 1 i.e. Avoid starvation.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The idiom "keep the wolf from the door" means to have just enough money to avoid hunger or starvation; to ward off poverty or want. (भुखमरी से बचना)
◦ Example: He took up a second job just to keep the wolf from the door.

• The idiom evokes the image of a hungry wolf prowling at one's door, symbolising the threat of hunger/poverty, which one manages to keep at bay through basic means.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 1.

Additional Information

• Option 2: "Wallow in poverty" (गरीबी में डूबे रहना): To be deeply and helplessly sunk in poverty — this is nearly the opposite of "keeping the wolf away".

• Option 3: "Relish food" (भोजन का आनंद लेना): To enjoy food greatly — unrelated to the idiom's sense of bare survival.

• Option 4: "Encourage starvation" (भुखमरी को बढ़ावा देना): The direct opposite of the idiom's actual meaning.

NOTE

• Other idioms about poverty/survival often asked by SSC: "live from hand to mouth" (to have barely enough money to live on), "make both ends meet" (to manage with limited money), "on the breadline" (living in poverty).

question:
Select the most appropriate ANTONYM of the given word.
Entire
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 3 i.e. Incomplete.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• "Entire" means whole; complete, with no part left out. (संपूर्ण)
◦ Example: She spent the entire day reading.

• "Incomplete" means not complete; lacking some part(s) (अपूर्ण), which is the direct opposite of "entire".

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 3.

Additional Information

• Option 1: Ingress (प्रवेश): The act of entering, or the right/means of entry — unrelated in meaning to "entire".

• Option 2: Thorough (पूर्ण/गहन): Complete in every detail; careful and exhaustive — this is actually a synonym, not an antonym, of "entire".

• Option 4: Undivided (अविभाजित): Not divided or shared; whole — this is also a synonym of "entire", not its antonym.

NOTE

• Synonyms of "entire": whole, complete, total, undivided, intact, thorough. Antonyms of "entire": incomplete, partial, fragmentary, deficient.

question:
Select the most appropriate option that can substitute the underlined segment in the given sentence. If no substitution is required, select 'No substitution'.
No matter how hard work you, your boss will not recognise your efforts.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 1 i.e. hard you work.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• In a clause beginning with "No matter how", the correct word order is "No matter how + adjective/adverb + subject + verb".

• Rule: "No matter how" is followed directly by the adjective/adverb (here, "hard"), and then the subject-verb order ("you work") — i.e. "No matter how hard you work".

• Applying the rule, the jumbled segment "hard work you," must be corrected to "hard you work,", giving "No matter how hard you work, your boss will not recognise your efforts."

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 1.

Additional Information

• Option 2: "work you do hard" is incorrect; it awkwardly separates "hard" from immediately following "how" and does not fit the required "how + adjective + subject + verb" pattern.

• Option 3: "hardly you work" is incorrect because "hardly" means "barely/scarcely" and completely changes the intended meaning of the sentence (which is about working with great effort, not barely working).

• Option 4: "no substitution" is incorrect because the original segment "hard work you," has a clear word-order error that needs correction.

NOTE

• "No matter how/what/who/where/when" clauses always take the pattern: No matter + wh-word + adjective/noun/adverb + subject + verb, e.g. "No matter what you say", "No matter who comes", "No matter how difficult it is". Also remember "hard" (adverb: with great effort) vs "hardly" (adverb: barely/scarcely) are commonly confused.

question:
Select the most appropriate option that can substitute the underlined segment in the given sentence.
My cousin works day and night to achieve success in life.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 2 i.e. around the clock.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The phrase "day and night" means continuously; all the time, without stopping. (दिन-रात, लगातार)
◦ Example: The nurses worked day and night to care for the patients.

• "Around the clock" means continuously, throughout the day and night, without a break (चौबीसों घंटे), which is an exact idiomatic match for "day and night".
◦ Example: The factory operates around the clock to meet demand.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 2.

Additional Information

• Option 1: "vale of tears" (दुखों का संसार): An idiom referring to the sorrows and troubles of earthly life — unrelated in meaning.

• Option 3: "great dealing" is not a standard English idiom/phrase and does not fit the sentence.

• Option 4: "a handful" (मुट्ठी भर/कठिन व्यक्ति): A small quantity, or informally, a person/thing that is difficult to manage — unrelated in meaning.

NOTE

• Other idioms meaning "continuously/without stop": "round the clock", "day in day out", "morning, noon and night", "non-stop".

question:
Select the word OPPOSITE in meaning to the underlined word in the given sentence.
Feeling discouraged, she finally finds the motivation for pursing her goal.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 1 i.e. inspired.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• "Discouraged" means having lost confidence or enthusiasm; disheartened. (हतोत्साहित)
◦ Example: He felt discouraged after failing the test twice.

• "Inspired" means filled with the urge or ability to do or feel something, especially something creative; motivated and encouraged (प्रेरित), which is the direct opposite of "discouraged" — the sentence itself confirms this, as she "finds the motivation" despite initially feeling discouraged.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 1.

Additional Information

• Option 2: "energetic" (ऊर्जावान): Having or showing physical/mental energy — related to enthusiasm but not a precise opposite of "discouraged" (one can be discouraged yet still energetic, or encouraged yet tired).

• Option 3: "admired" (प्रशंसित): Regarded with respect or approval — unrelated in meaning to "discouraged".

• Option 4: "disappointed" (निराश): Feeling let down due to unmet expectations — this is close in meaning to "discouraged", not its opposite.

NOTE

• Synonyms of "discouraged": disheartened, demoralised, dispirited, disappointed. Antonyms: encouraged, inspired, motivated, heartened.

question:
In the following passage, some words have been deleted. Read the passage carefully and select the most appropriate option to fill in each blank.

I have a recurring dream. Actually, I have a few: one is about dismembering a body , I'd rather not get into it, but the (1)_________ pertinent one is about college. It's the end of the semester, and I suddenly (2)_________ that there is a class I forgot to attend, ever, and now I have to sit for the final exam. I wake up panicked, my GPA in peril. How could I have done this? Why do I so (3)_________ dissatisfy myself? Then I remember I haven't been in college in more than a decade.
Someone with (4)_________ knowledge of my academic career might point out that this nightmare scenario is not that far removed from my actual collegiate experience, and that at certain times in my life, it did not take the magic of slumber to find me completely unprepared for a final. And, well, (5)_________ of what may or may not be true of my personal scholastic rigour, I suspect the school-stress dream is quite a common one.

Select the most appropriate option to fill in blank number 1.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 4 i.e. more.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The sentence compares TWO dreams the writer has: one about dismembering a body, and one about college. Since only two things are being compared, the COMPARATIVE degree of the adjective/adverb must be used, not the superlative.

• Rule: When comparing exactly two items, use the comparative form ("more ___" / "___-er"); the superlative form ("most ___" / "___-est") is used only when comparing three or more items.

• Applying the rule: since only two recurring dreams are being compared, "the more pertinent one" (comparative) is correct, not "the best pertinent one" or "the strong pertinent one".

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 4.

Additional Information

• Option 1: "better" is grammatically a comparative form, but it does not collocate with "pertinent" — English does not use "better pertinent"; the correct comparative of a multi-syllable adjective like "pertinent" is formed with "more", not "better".

• Option 2: "best" is the superlative form, which is incorrect here since only two dreams are being compared, not three or more.

• Option 3: "strong" is the positive (base) degree of the adjective, and also does not fit the sense of "pertinent" (relevant) being compared here.

NOTE

• For adjectives of two or more syllables (e.g. "pertinent", "beautiful", "important"), the comparative is usually formed with "more" and the superlative with "most", rather than adding "-er"/"-est".

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The blank describes the writer suddenly becoming aware, within the dream, that there is a class they forgot to attend — this sense of "suddenly becoming aware/conscious of a fact" is best expressed by the verb "realise".

• Rule (context-based vocabulary): The correct word must fit logically with what follows: "...that there is a class I forgot to attend...". Only "realise that + clause" naturally expresses becoming aware of a fact.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The blank describes the depth of "knowledge of my academic career" that a hypothetical "someone" might have. "Remote" here means slight, faint, or not close/detailed (a "remote knowledge" = only a slight, vague familiarity), which fits the writer's self-deprecating tone about their limited real academic record.

• Rule (context/collocation): "Remote" collocates naturally with abstract nouns like "knowledge", "chance", "possibility", "connection" to mean "slight/faint", a common usage tested in vocabulary-based cloze passages.

• Applying this, "Someone with remote knowledge of my academic career" means someone who knows only a little, vague amount about it — fitting the sentence's continuation about how the nightmare is "not that far removed" from reality.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 3.

Additional Information

• Option 1: "instigate" is a verb (to bring about or provoke an action) and cannot grammatically fit as an adjective before "knowledge".

• Option 2: "distant" is close in meaning but less idiomatic than "remote" when paired with "knowledge" in standard usage; "remote knowledge/chance/possibility" is the more natural collocation tested here.

• Option 4: "bleak" means "depressing, without hope", which does not fit the sense of "a small amount of knowledge".

NOTE

• "Remote" is frequently used idiomatically to mean "slight/faint" with abstract nouns: a remote chance, a remote possibility, a remote connection. Do not confuse this sense with its literal meaning of "far away in physical distance".

Select the most appropriate option to fill in blank number 5.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 3 i.e. regardless.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The blank is immediately followed by the word "of" — "___ of what may or may not be true...". Among the options, only "regardless" forms the standard fixed phrase "regardless of", meaning "without being affected by; irrespective of".

• Rule (fixed phrase/collocation): "Regardless" is always followed by "of" ("regardless of"); "nevertheless" and "notwithstanding" are not conventionally followed directly by "of" in this way, and "inasmuch" is used only in the fixed phrase "inasmuch as", never "inasmuch of".

• Applying this, "regardless of what may or may not be true of my personal scholastic rigour" is the only grammatically correct and idiomatic option.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 3.

Additional Information

• Option 1: "nevertheless" is a standalone conjunctive adverb (meaning "however/in spite of that") and is not followed by "of"; "nevertheless of" is not standard English.

• Option 2: "notwithstanding" can be used as a preposition ("notwithstanding this") but is not conventionally followed by "of"; "notwithstanding of" is not idiomatic.

• Option 4: "inasmuch" only occurs in the fixed phrase "inasmuch as" (meaning "since/because"), never as "inasmuch of"; it therefore cannot fit before "of".

NOTE

• Commonly confused connectors: "regardless of" (irrespective of), "in spite of" / "despite" (without being affected by, despite does not take "of"), "notwithstanding" (in spite of, used before or after the noun), "inasmuch as" (since/because).
